items.title: Oil plunges, stock futures surge after U.S.-Iran ceasefire

featured_image.name: Oil prices plunge below $100 after Iran agrees to safe passage through Strait of Hormuz during ceasefire

items.description: Oil prices plummeted below $100 a barrel and U.S. stock futures jumped on Tuesday evening after President Donald Trump announced a two-week ceasefire with Iran, pulling back from an 8 p.m. ET deadline that had threatened the destruction of Iranian civilian infrastructure. The announcement, made on Truth Social around 6:30 p.m. ET, marked a dramatic reversal from hours of escalating threats that had rattled global markets throughout the day.[1][2][3]

The work, published on Monday in Nature Physics, blurs the line between engineered objects and living systems.[1][2]

items.title: China helped push Iran to accept ceasefire, AP reports

featured_image.name: China emerges as 'potential guarantor' in Iran-US talks amid Pakistan  diplomacy

items.description:
Hours before President Donald Trump's deadline for Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz expired on Tuesday, a two-week ceasefire was announced — and behind the scenes, China appears to have played a quiet but critical role in getting Tehran to the table.

According to the Associated Press, Chinese officials were in direct contact with their Iranian counterparts as ceasefire negotiations evolved, encouraging Tehran to find a path toward a deal. The New York Times reported that Iran faced pressure from China to accept Pakistan's two-week truce proposal, while the New York Post, citing Iranian officials, said China joined Pakistan in urging Iran to agree.[1][2][3][4][5]

items.title: Israel backs US-Iran ceasefire but excludes Lebanon fight

featured_image.name: Netanyahu orders military to expand invasion of southern Lebanon

items.description:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu endorsed President Donald Trump's decision to suspend airstrikes on Iran for two weeks, but made clear that the deal does not extend to Israel's military operations against Hezbollah in Lebanon, setting up a potential fault line in the fragile truce before negotiations have even begun.

The announcement came on Tuesday after Trump pulled back from his threat to destroy Iran's bridges, power plants, and civilian infrastructure, declaring a mutual ceasefire contingent on Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Israel agreed to the terms of the two-week ceasefire, according to the Associated Press, citing a White House official. But Netanyahu's office stressed that the agreement applies only to the Iran front — not to Lebanon, where Israeli forces have been conducting a grinding campaign against the Iranian-backed militant group since early March.[1][2][3]

items.title: North Korea fires projectile a day after rare diplomatic thaw

featured_image.name: Suspected North Korean missile launch 'failed,' possibly ...

items.description:
North Korea launched an unidentified projectile from its capital area on Tuesday, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff confirmed on Wednesday, in a move that came just one day after South Korean President Lee Jae Myung expressed regret over drone incursions into the North.[1][2]

The JCS said it detected the launch from the Pyongyang region and that South Korean and U.S. intelligence authorities are analyzing the projectile, without providing further details. The projectile, believed to have been fired in the morning, apparently failed shortly after launch, according to the Korea Times, citing Yonhap.[3][1]

items.title: Physical crude hits all-time high as Hormuz crisis deepens

featured_image.name: Strait Of Hormuz Standoff Threatens Global Oil Supply - Grand Pinnacle  Tribune

items.description:
The price of physical crude oil surged to all-time highs on Tuesday, with some grades nearing $150 a barrel as European and Asian refiners scrambled for immediate supply, underscoring the severity of the energy crisis triggered by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

Dated Brent, the benchmark used to price much of the world's physical crude, reached a record $144.42 per barrel on Tuesday afternoon, surpassing levels seen during both the 2008 financial crisis and Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, according to data compiled by S&P Global Platts. North Sea Forties crude climbed to $146.09 a barrel, also an all-time high, according to LSEG data. When the Platts dated Brent assessment is used as a base, many physical cargoes effectively priced above $150 a barrel.[1][2][3][4][5]

items.title: US and Iran set for pivotal peace talks Friday in Islamabad

featured_image.name: US, Iran to pause war, agree to 2-week ceasefire

items.description:
Iran's Supreme National Security Council confirmed that formal negotiations with the United States will begin on Friday, April 10, in Islamabad, following a dramatic two-week ceasefire announced by President Donald Trump on Tuesday evening just 90 minutes before his own deadline to launch devastating strikes on Iranian infrastructure.[1][2][3]

The SNSC, in a statement posted to its Telegram channel, said Iran would enter the talks with "complete distrust of the American side" and stressed that agreeing to negotiate "does not mean the end of the war". Iran has allocated up to two weeks for the negotiations, with the possibility of extension by mutual agreement.[4][5]

items.title: Dated Brent surges to record $144 as Iran war chokes supply

featured_image.name: Dated Brent Oil Price Jumps to Highest Level on Record ...

items.description:
Physical oil prices hit an all-time high on Tuesday as the war in Iran, now in its sixth week, continues to choke global crude supply through the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Dated Brent, the benchmark for North Sea crude bought and sold for near-term delivery, soared above $144 a barrel — the highest level since the pricing series began in 1987, according to Bloomberg.[1][2]

The record in physical prices underscores the growing desperation among refiners scrambling to secure barrels for immediate delivery, even as Brent futures for June settled lower near $109 a barrel on Tuesday. The widening gap between spot and futures prices reflects a market where traders are paying steep premiums for crude they can get their hands on now.[1]

items.title: Oil prices drop as Pakistan-brokered ceasefire pauses US-Iran strikes

featured_image.name: U.S. oil price plunges 14% to below $100 after Trump agrees to two-week ceasefire in Iran war

items.description: Six weeks of war between the United States and Iran have sent oil prices soaring past $100 a barrel, fueling the sharpest inflation fears since 2023 and forcing the Federal Reserve into a holding pattern on interest rates. On Tuesday, a last-minute two-week ceasefire brokered by Pakistan offered a glimmer of relief — crude prices dropped sharply in evening trading — but economists warn the damage to consumer confidence and the inflation outlook may already be done.
